This document is the project's internal map — per-paper summaries of every settled position, and the consolidated register of every question the series has and has not yet closed. It is written for researchers and returning readers who want to understand how the papers relate, what version each is at, and where the open edges of the argument are. It does not introduce new positions or resolve any open question.

First-time readers should start with [Start Here](start-here.html) instead.

## 1. The Whitepaper (WP)

The WDT taxes the annual change ("delta") in an individual's net worth above an exemption threshold, on an accrual basis, with three interdependent mechanical components plus one governance extension: an accrual-basis tax on annual wealth deltas at progressive marginal rates; a symmetric loss-refund mechanism under which the state refunds a proportional share of wealth losses at the same marginal rate that would have applied to an equivalent gain; a pre-funded Sovereign Wealth Fund (SWF) that capitalises the refund obligation; and governance participation by the taxpayer population in the SWF's institutional design.

The tax base is the annual change in net worth assessed across a taxpayer-elected assessment window (one to seven years), assessed at fair market value on a fixed annual date. The unit of taxation is the individual. Progressive rates apply marginally to the delta; refund rates in loss years mirror the gain-year marginal rate. Cumulative lifetime refunds cannot exceed cumulative lifetime taxes paid: the lifetime contribution envelope. A high exemption threshold excludes the substantial majority of households, justified on administrative-cost grounds and, per MF, on a moral judgment about differential capacity to bear bad years.

Assessment window elections reduce single-year valuation noise and the frequency of cash settlement events without changing total tax owed across a window; longer windows carry a deferral charge plus flexibility levy, both Governing Council parameters. The valuation architecture (detailed in VAL) works on the principle that because a declared value establishes the recognised basis for all future deltas, understatement defers tax rather than eliminating it. The SWF pre-funds the refund liability, invested in low-correlation assets. The Route D auction mechanism (detailed in GOV §6.1 and GOV.B §G) provides a Harberger-derived deterrent of last resort for egregious self-declarations on Route D; a Valuation Body consensus triggers an open auction at the declared price, third parties bid competitively, the taxpayer holds a right of first refusal at the highest third-party bid price, and the winning price becomes the new recognised basis. It is a credibility mechanism, not an allocative one.

The cooperative architecture rests on three convergent arguments: the moral argument that reciprocal treatment of gains and losses is a requirement of fair dealing; the incentive argument that reciprocal protections alter the rational calculus of the population best positioned to resist the system; and the political-durability argument that a system perceived as adversarial will face more organised opposition than one offering reciprocal protections. These arguments are analytically distinct and none is claimed to be sufficient alone. A fourth constraint operates alongside the three (§1.1, added v2.1): the mechanism must not create regulatory dependencies on other economic systems. The WDT produces effects on surrounding structures — capital allocation, private credit markets, corporate financing, asset valuation — but none require co-legislation or forced restructuring. Every adaptation follows from adjusting to a different measurement point for wealth change. The corporate instrument requires companies to report a delta and issue shareholder statements; corporate structure and financing are untouched. Position closure works through the SWF's bridging facility within existing legal machinery, without requiring jurisdictions to harmonise exit taxation regimes. The delta base is self-contained; surrounding systems absorb its effects through ordinary market adjustment.

The governing objective is not redistribution but the preservation of the democratic conditions under which advanced capitalism remains legitimate and sustainable. The labour tax relief dividend is the mechanism through which that goal is actually pursued: an implementation that taxed wealth deltas successfully but directed revenue away from reducing the burden on labour income would satisfy the fiscal mechanics while failing on its own terms.

The implementation pathway has two phases. Phase One operates at a high threshold and low rate affecting a small population; it builds valuation infrastructure, capitalises the SWF, and generates Phase One behavioural evidence before the system scales. Phase Two lowers the threshold, raises rates, and delivers the labour tax relief dividend at scale. The transition between phases is gated by conditions (infrastructure reliability, SRR fill, LRR fill) rather than a fixed calendar.

The corporate instrument exists because for large listed companies with dispersed ownership, individual-level attribution is impractical at scale; the instrument is a collection mechanism, not a separate tax on corporations as taxable subjects. Private companies remain entirely within individual WDT assessment.

§8.7 (added v2.0) addresses the complexity objection: the claim that sophisticated taxpayers can always engineer their affairs to achieve genuine economic benefit while avoiding legal attribution. The WDT's response is structural rather than defensive. Conventional tax avoidance is substantially a legal-category game that exploits gaps between differently-rated or differently-timed tax bases. The WDT removes most of these gaps by changing the fundamental question from *what legal form was used* to *where did the wealth go*. Interposing a holding company achieves nothing because the delta flows through regardless of how many layers sit between the owner and the underlying assets. Deliberate opacity bears $\tau_m$ as a final charge, more expensive than the rate identifiable beneficiaries would face. The conditions required to defeat the WDT through structural means — simultaneously possessing genuine durable benefit, maintaining effective control, and holding no attributable asset or claim — are mutually incompatible. The detailed treatment of entity types and ownership structures is in CORP.A §F. Market manipulation is also addressed: a short position's gain is a bilateral claim between counterparties, not a claim on the reference company, so the "short → destroy → resurrect" strategy achieves nothing and artificial inflation attacks are self-correcting through the delta mechanism. The full treatment of market manipulation is in CORP.A §F.9.

## 2. The Moral and Philosophical Foundations Paper (MF)

The foundational axiom is that individual human beings are the only legitimate moral subjects of a tax system. Corporations, trusts, and funds are instruments through which human wealth is organised; they have no welfare of their own. This axiom generates all subsequent design choices.

Where wealth comes from: extraordinary wealth is partly a collective product, depending on the labour and consumption of the broader population and the public infrastructure their taxes fund. The connection between individual effort and financial return weakens at extreme concentration, where large fortunes emerge substantially from inheritance, structural positioning within ownership networks, and the compounding of advantages already held.

Wealth as power, not deferred consumption: above a threshold of basic sufficiency, wealth confers present-tense advantages independent of whether it is ever spent. The consumption-tax tradition's framing of wealth as deferred consumption becomes less convincing at extreme scale, where holdings may never be meaningfully consumed. The WDT treats wealth as durable economic and institutional power that exists and operates in the present.

The cognitive moral hazard of the current system: tax systems that make wage and consumption taxation visible while obscuring how unrealised wealth compounds do not produce neutral political outcomes. Making the relationship between concentrated wealth and the society enabling it observable is a precondition for better democratic deliberation, not a determination of what conclusions should be drawn.

The terminal goal is democratic flourishing, not equality of outcome. The WDT aims to maintain the conditions under which democratic institutions remain functional and ordinary people retain meaningful participation in the societies their labour and consumption sustain. It tolerates significant wealth concentration; it does not tolerate concentration so extreme that it captures the institutional conditions democratic legitimacy depends on.

The cooperative architecture is derived from the same foundational axiom — reciprocity is a requirement of fair dealing — not a political concession attached to the mechanism afterward. The state accepting downside exposure alongside the taxpayer through the symmetric refund is not a revenue-smoothing feature but the operational expression of that commitment.

The named compromises in MF §9 are the points at which theoretical purity and practical design part company, stated as trade-offs rather than natural extensions of the theory: the corporate instrument is justified on coverage grounds rather than on the individual-centred moral logic; asymmetric treatment of corporate loss years is principled (corporations do not experience losses in any humanly meaningful sense); the exemption threshold is partly an administrative necessity; international mobility creates a gap the system manages rather than closes; the system depends on functioning democratic institutions as a boundary condition it cannot itself supply; the transition period approximates rather than achieves the prospective-participation ideal; and the institutional tiers the mechanism produces (§9.7) — the formal distinctions between participants and non-participants, between long-tenure and new entrants, between dividend recipients and the general public — are visible, obligated, and democratically constrained, but tiers nonetheless. Whether they remain compatible with democratic flourishing is a wager rather than a guarantee, contingent on the robustness of the surrounding democratic institutions the WDT cannot itself supply.

The state/taxpayer relationship under cooperative architecture is characterised, per GOV.A §E.2, as reciprocal partnership: the state accepts downside exposure alongside the taxpayer rather than participating only in gains. This framing is the settled working characterisation across the project.

## 3. The Systematic Literature Review (LR) (Superceeded)

LR surveys the intellectual traditions the WDT draws on without proposing design positions of its own. Its principal findings, used across other papers, are these.

The cross-country empirical literature on wealth taxes is consistent: behavioural response magnitude is driven primarily by the quality of third-party reporting and the degree of jurisdictional arbitrage available, not by headline rates. Systems with strong reporting and national administration produce modest real responses; larger apparent responses typically reflect avoidance enabled by weak infrastructure (most clearly demonstrated in the Colombia evidence from Londono-Velez and Avila-Mahecha, 2024).

The Norway evidence (Kleven et al., 2024) finds approximately 22 cents of revenue lost per unit raised from migration following a wealth tax increase, with overall revenues still growing. A structural qualification applies: Agrawal, Foremny, and Martinez-Toledano (2025) find that wealth-tax-driven migration generates income tax and VAT losses approximately six times larger than the direct wealth-tax revenue loss. This cross-base externality disappears in a mature Phase Two context where those taxes no longer operate in parallel but remains unresolved for Phase One.

The Domar-Musgrave (1944) tradition and parallel work by Sandmo (1977), Stiglitz (1969), and King (1977) establish that symmetric government participation in investment outcomes reduces variance penalties on risky investment — but none of this literature has been formally extended to a progressive, delta-based wealth tax.

The Guvenen et al. (2023) "use-it-or-lose-it" efficiency argument establishes that wealth taxation can outperform capital income taxation on efficiency grounds when returns are heterogeneous across investors, but this was demonstrated for a stock wealth tax; the extension to a delta-based base has not been made.

The cooperative-compliance literature (Tyler, 1990; Kirchler, 2007; Gangl et al., 2015) supports the general claim that perceived procedural fairness improves compliance outcomes, but direct evidence for this mechanism among high-wealth, professionally-advised taxpayers does not exist. LR §7.2 develops this gap substantively: at the wealth levels where WDT revenue concentrates, the compliance decision is made within an institutional network of advisers, family offices, and trustees rather than by an individual taxpayer directly, and the cooperative architecture's behavioural effect is therefore primarily mediated through professional intermediaries. Adjacent literature (OECD Cooperative Compliance programme; Levi and Rothstein on elite legitimacy; Klepper and Nagin on adviser norm transmission) supports the directional claim without constituting direct evidence; Phase One is the resolution path.

No existing sovereign wealth fund model has governance participation by the tax-contributing population. The mutual insurance analogy (Hansmann, 2022) is the closest structural precedent, and it is an imperfect one.

The valuation insurance mechanism proposed in VAL has no identified precedent in the professional insurance literature.

LR's own seven research gaps all remain open. They are incorporated into the consolidated register in §9. Two companion papers have now been added to the LR cluster: LR.A formally diagnoses the nine confirmed gaps in the existing scholarly literature that bear directly on the WDT, distinguishing them from fresh questions created by the WDT's novelty and from Phase One empirical questions that require implementation data; LR.B provides the full source treatment for external references cited across the companion paper series, organised by problem rather than by tradition, with forward notes pointing to the WDT papers that develop or respond to each body of scholarship. These two papers together replace the function that LR §12 served as a brief research-gap register, at a level of detail the main LR paper does not carry.

## 3a. The Research Gaps Paper (LR.A)

LR.A is a diagnostic document, not a survey. Its purpose is to establish precisely where the existing academic literature has engaged with problems relevant to the WDT and stopped — left formally unresolved, not because the questions are unanswerable in principle, but because the specific modelling, evidence-gathering, or analytical extension has not been carried out. It identifies nine confirmed gaps, organises them by type, states what each gap consists of, and specifies what closing it would require.

The paper distinguishes three categories that must be kept distinct: genuine literature gaps (what LR.A covers), fresh questions created by the WDT's own novelty, and Phase One empirical questions requiring a live system. The nine confirmed gaps span three domains.

**Formal modelling gaps (§2).** The Domar-Musgrave variance-reduction result has not been formally extended to a progressive, delta-based wealth tax — the existing results are derived for flat-rate income taxation with loss offsets, and the three complications introduced by the delta base (net worth rather than asset return, progressive rates, multi-period asymmetry between gain-year and loss-year marginal rates) have not been addressed. The welfare comparison relevant to the WDT — delta base versus consumption tax alternative, at current concentration levels, on both efficiency and distributional grounds — has not been done; the Guvenen et al. (2023) use-it-or-lose-it model is calibrated to a stock wealth tax and has not been extended to a flow base. The distributional arithmetic of how a delta tax base concentrates revenue under persistent heterogeneous returns and the wealth-return gradient has not been formalised.

**Compliance and behavioural gaps (§3).** Direct compliance evidence for cooperative design effects at the ultra-high-net-worth level, among professionally mediated taxpayers, does not exist — the Tyler/Kirchler literature models individuals, but at the wealth levels where WDT revenue concentrates the compliance decision is made within institutional networks of advisers and family offices; whether cooperative design features alter adviser compliance postures is unaddressed. The cross-base migration externality identified by Agrawal et al. (2025) — income tax and VAT losses approximately six times larger than the direct wealth-tax revenue loss — has not been incorporated into any existing wealth tax behavioural model; standard revenue projections use direct-channel elasticities and systematically understate total fiscal cost. Whether specific administrative-layer interventions produce measurable effects on compliance psychology has not been studied; the question is partly Phase One dependent but is independently a gap in the literature's agenda.

**Political and international gaps (§4).** The three-mechanism causal framework for wealth tax abolition (legitimacy collapse, organised opposition advantage, institutional brittleness) derivable from Perret (2021) and the historical record has not been independently validated — it is an analytical construction requiring independent formal or comparative-case derivation. The political dimension of the international competitive dynamic — how economic mobility pressure transmits through domestic institutional channels to produce political outcomes — is unaddressed; the economics literature and the Zucman coordination proposals treat the fiscal externality without modelling its political conversion. The interaction between a refund-based system and a minimum-tax floor standard has not been addressed; no prior refund-based wealth tax has existed as a coordination reference point, so whether a negative-tax year constitutes a floor breach and how averaging would handle it is an open technical and legal design question.

LR.A does not generate new open questions for the §9 register. Its nine gaps are characterisations of the existing literature's limits, not design questions internal to the WDT. The corresponding WDT-internal open questions already in the §9 register — #2 (Domar-Musgrave extension), #3 (welfare comparison), #15 (cross-base externality), #16 (minimum-tax interaction), #17 (compliance evidence at high-wealth level), POL-1 (causal framework validation), POL-2 (international competitive dynamic at political level) — are the WDT project's responses to these literature gaps; they were already in the register before LR.A. LR.A confirms that those items are genuine gaps, not merely open design choices.

## 3b. The Intellectual Background and Reference Guide (LR.B)

LR.B is the reference guide to the intellectual ancestry of the WDT. Its nineteen sections cover the bodies of scholarship the project draws on, organised around the problems those bodies address rather than by intellectual tradition or by author. Each section is self-contained: it states what the relevant literature says, where its findings are robust, where they are contested, and where they stop. A forward note at the end of each section directs the reader to the companion papers that develop or respond to the ideas covered. The paper does not make arguments of its own and does not summarise what the WDT does.

LR.B is the publicly readable version of the source material in the project's master reference database (0.4). It is generated from 0.4 after that database is clean; it is not drafted in parallel with 0.4. All companion papers cite LR.B for their external references rather than carrying independent literature surveys. The companion gap register is LR.A.

The nineteen sections and their subject matter are: (1) introduction and how to use the document; (2) the tax base question — Haig-Simons, consumption tax, stock wealth tax; (3) unrealised gains and prior accrual proposals — Shakow, Auerbach, Vickrey, contemporary US proposals, contemporary legal scholarship; (4) symmetric loss treatment and risk-sharing — Domar-Musgrave, Sandmo, Stiglitz, King; (5) heterogeneous returns and efficiency — Fagereng et al., Guvenen et al., Piketty/Saez/Zucman 2023; (6) welfare comparisons — Chamley-Judd, Straub-Werning, Bradford, Viard-Carroll, Dias et al.; (7) the empirical wealth tax record — Sweden, Denmark, Norway, Switzerland, Colombia, concentration data; (8) the valuation problem — Shakow, IVSC, Pereira Gray Review, Advani/Chamberlain/Summers; (9) self-assessment and deterrence — Harberger, Posner-Weyl, Weyl-Zhang; (10) cooperative compliance and procedural justice — Tyler, Kirchler, Gangl et al., Ayres-Braithwaite, Kleven et al. 2011; (11) compliance in professionally mediated systems — Klepper-Nagin, Erard, Sakurai-Braithwaite, OECD Cooperative Compliance, Levi, Rothstein, Kornhauser, Richardson; (12) collective action and governance of multi-constituency institutions — Olson, Ostrom, Fung-Wright, Fishkin; (13) mutual and pension governance — Hansmann, O'Sullivan, MacMinn-Ren, ICMIF, Clark-Urwin, Ambachtsheer; (14) sovereign wealth fund reference cases — GPFG/Norway, Truman, Frankel, Aizenman-Glick, Chile, Alaska; (15) precommitment and fiscal rules — Kydland-Prescott, Elster, Kopits-Symansky, Wyplosz, Debrun et al.; (16) moral philosophy and the normative case — Murphy-Nagel, Rawls, Atkinson, Galbraith, Mills, Hacker-Pierson; (17) democratic legitimacy and wealth concentration — Dahl, Bartels, Gilens, Piketty/Saez/Zucman 2023; (18) exit taxation and international coordination — OECD 2025, European Commission 2026, Jakobsen et al. 2024, Kleven/Landais/Muñoz/Stantcheva, Agrawal et al. 2025, Zucman 2024; (19) orphaned references — holding area for sources not yet assigned to §§2–18.

LR.B does not generate new open questions for the §9 register. It is a reference document, not a position paper.

## 4. The Valuation Companion Papers (VAL, VAL.A, VAL.B)

The central reframing: the valuation problem for annual wealth taxation has been incorrectly stated. The question is not how the state discovers the correct value of an asset a taxpayer prefers to undervalue. The question is under what conditions understatement ceases to be the rational strategy — and what the actual equilibrium looks like. The design objective is to remove any systematic rational preference for understatement. The mechanism achieves this not by making honest declaration dominant but by making mild overstatement dominant: understatement carries definite, compounding costs; mild overstatement (α ≈ 1.2–1.5) carries a permanent, forecast-independent TW advantage; and aggressive overstatement is self-limiting through a growth-corridor mechanism. Honest declaration remains the only strategy with no forecast exposure at all, but it is not the equilibrium the mechanism produces.

The delta-based self-correction is the mechanism achieving this: because a declared value establishes the recognised basis for all future deltas, understatement defers tax rather than eliminating it, and the cost compounds with asset growth. The simulation model is calibrated to RATES-aligned parameters ($V_0$ = £20m, $\tau_0$ = 15%, $\tau_m$ = 70%, W_min = £2m, k = 0.001, N = 29). **Python model v1.0 validation is complete. VAL.A v3.1 §C contains confirmed figures (0 FAILs across all primary matrices) at unified parameters (N = 29 following RATES budget_growth correction to 4.51%). VAL.B v1.5 contains five worked examples (§J–§N) at N = 32 — one version behind VAL.A v3.1; a VAL.B update to N = 29 is pending. The directional claims stand as stated: understatement is more expensive than honest declaration across the policy-relevant growth range; mild overstatement (α ≈ 1.2–1.5) produces a permanent, forecast-independent TW advantage; aggressive overstatement (α ≥ 1.8) is self-limiting through a growth-corridor mechanism. Table C.3 carries deviations up to 13% at extreme α×β values due to exponential compounding; directional claims unaffected. VAL.A v2.7 corrected the rate function formula in §A.3.1, §A.4.2, §B.2 (τ_m now correctly in numerator; A redefined as (τ_m − τ_0)/τ_0). VAL.A v2.8 corrected derivation steps in §A.4.2 and §A.4.4 against the Python model; §B.4 metric C.1 formula sign corrected. VAL.A v2.9 removed the Limitations section and added a design note to §A.3.2 on refund marginal rate choice. VAL.A v3.0 updated τ₀ = 15%, N = 32 and replaced all §C tables. VAL.A v3.1 updated N = 29 and replaced all §C tables; §C.4 rate ceiling updated to 60.67%. Current section structure: §E = Route Specification Tables; §F = Annual Reporting Requirements (prior §H and §I respectively; §F Limitations no longer exists).**

Assets are classified across two dimensions — fungible or non-fungible, and professionally valued or self-declared — producing four routes with different assessment, settlement, and deterrence mechanics.

Route A (professional, fungible) uses competitive-tender professional valuation with valuation risk sitting with the valuator. Route B (professional, non-fungible) follows the same professional structure with deferred cash settlement available as a lien and forced settlement at every change of ownership. Route C (self-declared, fungible) requires settlement in kind by transferring a proportional equity interest at the declared value; this must-transfer mechanism creates continuous active self-correction through dilution. Route D (self-declared, non-fungible) defers all taxation to realisation, because periodic cash settlement on illiquid assets would recreate forced-realisation pressure, and because in-kind settlement is impossible for non-fungible positions.

Taxpayers elect an assessment window of one to seven years; annual reporting continues throughout. A premium applies to longer windows (deferral charge plus flexibility levy), calibrated by the Governing Council once Phase One election data exists. The assessment window premium is excluded from RATES's reference revenue model.

Professional valuation uses a competitive-tender model (not client-appointed) with a two-stage review process and financial consequences for overturned valuators. The Valuation Code Board is an independent statutory body governing methodology.

The Route D auction mechanism (detailed in GOV §10) is available on Route D only. When the three-body Valuation Body consensus confirms an egregious entry understatement, the asset is offered at open auction at the taxpayer's own declared price; any party may bid, including the taxpayer; the winning price becomes the new recognised basis and generates a taxable delta in the auction year. The mechanism is a deterrent of last resort; it depends on occasional exercise for its credibility and is not a routine enforcement tool. Route C is excluded because the must-transfer settlement already creates continuous active self-correction through dilution throughout the holding period.

Voluntary settlement options on Route D (soft and hard basis resets) allow taxpayers to crystallise liability before a forced realisation event. The inheritance auction provides mandatory hard-basis-reset price discovery when a Route D asset passes to an heir.

VAL's stated limitations include: the Route D entry basis is the most vulnerable point — generally unverified, with limited deterrence where no reliable comparables exist; Route D lacks interim loss symmetry by design; and the high-growth boundary condition (the C.1 metric for α = 0.1 crosses 100% at approximately g = 23–24% at canonical parameters) is a normalisation artefact rather than a sign reversal — the understater's excess tax exceeds their own terminal wealth at extreme growth, but the penalty does not reverse. The understater penalty plateaus at g ≈ 17% (a property of the rate function, constant across all α) rather than reversing.

A refinement to the incentive framing is established in VAL.A v2.6 §A.6 (Proposition 6 / Finding 5). The stable equilibrium zone is mild overstatement at α ≈ 1.2–1.5, not exact honest declaration. The mechanism produces this outcome through two distinct structural features. First, understater penalties escalate steeply between g ≈ 10% and g ≈ 17% then plateau — the rate function's logistic ceiling stops the marginal deterrent from escalating further but does not reverse it, and the plateau ceiling scales proportionally with the degree of understatement. Second, mild overstatement (α ≤ 1.5) produces a TW advantage that is permanent and forecast-independent: it holds across the full tested growth range without requiring the taxpayer to be right about the asset's trajectory. Aggressive overstatement (α ≥ 1.8) faces a growth-corridor requirement — the bracket penalty dominates in the g ≈ 9–17% range containing the historical mean, so the advantage recovers only outside that corridor — and the maximum achievable TW benefit is bounded at approximately 12% regardless of how far α is pushed. Aggressive overstatement is therefore self-limiting through the mechanism's own structure rather than through any explicit deterrent. The population-level prediction is systematic mild overstatement as the declaration equilibrium, which is more robust than exact honest declaration since it emerges from rational self-interest under uncertainty. Three practical consequences follow: the declared tax base slightly exceeds true values, partially offsetting the pre-behavioural revenue overstatement in RATES; refund exposure in loss years is correspondingly larger, because refunds are calculated on declared bases (SRR floor calibration implication assigned as ENV-1); and the public register carries systematically inflated declared values during holding periods, creating a credit-expansion effect on private asset-backed lending through lenders and counterparties using register entries as reference points. There is currently no instrument through which the Governing Council can observe or respond to drift in the population distribution of declared values — this is a named monitoring gap. Phase One data on declared values relative to subsequent realisation prices is the primary detection mechanism.

VAL v2.5–v2.6 formalises the declaration-zone framing in the main paper itself: §7.1 and the Conclusion now explicitly characterise the white zone (α = 0.8 to 1.5 at historical mean growth) as a design feature rather than an enforcement gap, and six figures (Figs 5.1–5.2, 7.1–7.5) make the quantitative structure of the incentive landscape visually present in VAL, alongside the existing analytical treatment in VAL.A.

## 5. The UK Jurisdiction and Data Reference Paper (JUR)

JUR justifies the UK as reference jurisdiction and compiles the empirical data companion papers require. It does not design or modify the WDT.

The companion papers model an idealised country inheriting UK population and demographic data, UK tax revenue composition, and UK institutional architecture in outline (HMRC-like, OBR-like, VOA-like, specialist tax tribunal). What is not modelled: parliamentary sovereignty's specific legal mechanics, post-Brexit information exchange complications, devolution, and UK non-dom regime history.

The key institutional mapping: HMRC is the assumed administrative home for WDT operations, with adequate existing capacity in principle but no current infrastructure for annual net worth tracking. The VOA provides property valuations at scale but has no function for private company equity. The OBR model — a small statutory independent fiscal body with Treasury Select Committee oversight of appointments — is the principal precedent for the SWF Custodian's institutional form. The tax tribunal system is adequate in principle but under significant backlog pressure.

Key data: the top 1% of UK individuals holds approximately 23% of total wealth, possibly more (WAS undersamples above £3m and lost Official Statistics accreditation in June 2025). Approximately 32,000 UK individuals hold wealth above £10m. Income tax and National Insurance together raise approximately £475b annually — the primary taxes the WDT's revenue is intended to reduce the burden of.

The OBR independence stress test (the 2022 mini-budget period and December 2025 chair resignation) is reassigned to Phase One in JUR v1.6 §4.4. The structural design question of what properties a mandate-guardian institution needs is settled by GOV §6.3 (SWF Custodian). Whether the actual OBR meets those properties requires empirical data not available at the design stage; implementation will generate it. JUR carries no remaining open questions of its own. Note: JUR's body text retains cross-references to old GOV section numbers — §8.6 (mandate-guardian properties, now GOV §6.3) and §8.4 (institutional mapping, now GOV.B §E.6) — which predate the GOV v2.1 restructuring. These are stale but benign: the content they point to exists at the new locations.

## 6. The Corporate Architecture Paper (CORP) and Appendix (CORP.A)

The corporate instrument solves an attribution problem, not a valuation problem. For large listed companies with dispersed ownership across foreign holders, institutional pools, and below-threshold retail shareholders, individual-level attribution of annual market-cap appreciation is impractical at scale. Existing instruments — corporate income tax, capital gains tax, dividend taxation — do not capture retained, unrealised appreciation as it accrues.

CORP v2.0 §2 extends the insufficiency argument with an explicit efficiency case against corporate income tax and dividend taxation as a system. CIT falls on accounting profit — a construct with enormous discretion through transfer pricing, IP location, thin capitalisation, intragroup debt, and the retained-earnings bias from double-taxation of distributed profit. Share buybacks over dividends are a rate-arbitrage strategy with the same effect. The only serious argument for CIT as a system is collection security: it taxes corporate accumulation before wealth reaches identifiable individuals. That is a collection argument, not an efficiency argument, and it is the same argument the corporate delta levy makes — on a different and better base. The WDT corporate levy sidesteps these distortions because its base is annual market capitalisation change, not declared profit. Transfer pricing becomes irrelevant, income-to-capital conversion becomes irrelevant, and the debt preference partially dissolves.

The listed/private distinction is categorical. Private companies remain entirely within individual WDT assessment via VAL routes. Listed companies require the corporate delta levy.

The levy mechanism: the corporation calculates an annual market-capitalisation delta, pays a provisional levy into a settlement account, and issues delta statements to registered shareholders within sixty days. Native WDT shareholders include the allocated amount in their annual WDT assessment and claim a credit within a fixed one-year reconciliation window. The gap between the provisional rate and each shareholder's marginal rate flows to the tax authority through individual settlement automatically.

Ownership is divided into three tranches. Tranche one covers native shareholders, who receive hard legal credits. Tranche two covers identified intermediaries assessed against the attribution test: whether the intermediary can identify and attribute its underlying beneficiaries to a degree sufficient to support individual WDT reconciliation. Where it can, downstream pass-through to individual settlement is available; where it cannot, $\tau_0$ is final at the company level. Tranche three covers unidentified beneficial owners, who bear a higher final charge at $\tau_h$. Loss years generate no corporate levy and no corporate refund, because the corporate instrument's asymmetry follows directly from the individual-centred logic: shareholders experiencing losses are covered through their own individual assessments.

The attribution test determines treatment; entity type does not. DC pension schemes are excluded as a policy boundary (disproportionate infrastructure cost at the current threshold relative to the revenue at stake), not a principled failure of the attribution test. DB schemes are excluded on principled grounds: a DB member's claim is to a promised benefit, not a proportional share of fund NAV.

Derivatives and synthetic exposure are excluded from corporate-levy reconciliation. A derivative claim runs against a counterparty, not the company, so there is no corporate-level ledger position and no double-count risk arises.

Corporate lifecycle events are settled by design rule: IPO transitions, mergers and share-for-share exchanges, and share buybacks each have specified treatment in CORP §4.1. CORP v2.0 §4.1 adds three further categories. Thinly traded listed companies: where a nominally listed company falls below a liquidity threshold, it is reclassified to professional valuation under Route B rather than assessed through the corporate delta mechanism; the threshold is a Governing Council Tier 1 parameter informed by Phase One data on price volatility and assessment-date trading volumes. Suspended and delisted companies: mid-year suspension or delisting is a corporate position closure event; the assessment position closes, the final delta is calculated to the last reliable traded price, and the general position closure framework in CLOSE applies without a separate corporate rule; relisting reopens from an IPO basis. Dual-class share structures: delta is allocated to each share class proportionally to its economic entitlement per share, not its voting rights; delta statements must specify the per-class ratio used.

The rate framework was disaggregated in CORP v1.5 into two distinct optimisation problems, each developed further in CORP.A v1.5 and v1.6. $\tau_prov$ is an administrative cash-flow parameter whose floor ($\tau_0$) is grounded in collection-security against reconciliation failure: where a shareholder fails to settle within the reconciliation window, the provisional amount already held is the only recovery available. $\tau_0$ is calibrated against the expected revenue loss per assessment cycle from non-reconciliation — approximately the product of the non-reconciliation rate, the per-failure shortfall, and the tranche-one delta allocation. Structurally, the failure population clusters at lower wealth levels (large WDT taxpayers have strong incentive to reconcile), and the CLOSE bridging facility substantially reduces the emigration component; the result is that $\tau_0$ at or near the individual entry-level effective rate is likely to provide adequate collection security. Phase One data — non-reconciliation rates by wealth band and by reason — will allow the Governing Council to convert this initial calibration into a standing data-driven rule. The full framework is in CORP.A §B.1. $\tau_h$ is a final charge on permanently unattributable ownership. Its calibration range is [deterrence floor, $\tau_m$]: the floor is set by the deterrence condition net of the refund-forfeiture effect (permanently unattributed positions forfeit loss-year refunds, which partially substitutes for rate-based deterrence); the ceiling is $\tau_m$ on revenue-recovery grounds. Legal proportionality, previously identified as a competing downward pressure on $\tau_h$, is now assessed as substantially weaker than initially framed: mounting a legal challenge to $\tau_h$ requires establishing standing as beneficial owner, which is itself an attribution event triggering automatic reclassification to the correct tranche and dissolving $\tau_h$'s application. The "exit from $\tau_h$" route is always available and always within the claimant's control, which satisfies proportionality review without compressing the calibration range from above. The Governing Council holds genuine discretion within [deterrence floor, $\tau_m$], with Phase One attribution trend data — tranche-three share of corporate ownership over time, attribution test pass/fail rates by entity type — as the primary input to any revision. The RATES revenue model retains $\tau_c$ = $\tau_m$ = 70% as a working ceiling assumption for estimation purposes, consistent with the revised framework. The full derivation is in CORP.A §B.2.

CORP v2.0 adds §6, the **Corporate Equity Settlement Facility**, as an alternative to cash settlement of the provisional levy. The facility exists to resolve the timing mismatch between a tax base measured in market value and a settlement obligation requiring cash, which bears most acutely on companies whose market capitalisation has risen substantially because markets are pricing expected future earnings but whose operations are not yet cash-generative. As an alternative to cash settlement, any listed company may transfer shares to the SWF at market price. The SWF issues a loan to the company equal to the levy amount, secured against the transferred shares. The company repays from future cash flows at its own pace, subject to a minimum annual repayment schedule. A right of early repurchase exists at market price at any point; a margin call mechanism applies if collateral value falls below a defined threshold; at the maximum holding period, remaining held shares are sold into the market. Shares transferred through the facility are held in a distinct named portfolio within the SWF, separate from the SRR and from Route C equity positions. The facility's demand is structurally countercyclical: companies produce large positive deltas and face liquidity constraints in boom conditions — precisely when the SWF is accumulating assets most quickly — and the facility's positions are in rundown in bear years when the SWF's overall position is weakest. All parameters (pre-assessment transfer-price window, loan interest rate, minimum repayment schedule, margin call threshold, maximum holding period, and the liquidity threshold below which nominally listed companies route to Route B) are Governing Council Tier 1 calibration parameters informed by Phase One take-up data and the Custodian's portfolio risk assessment.

CORP.A v1.9 §B.2 adds a **$\tau_h$ ramp mechanism**. Rather than fixing $\tau_h$ at a single value from Phase One, the Governing Council publishes in advance a schedule under which $\tau_h$ rises from its initial level toward the ceiling of [deterrence floor, $\tau_m$] over a defined transition window, paced by observed aggregate attribution trends. The aggregate observable is the tranche-three share of listed corporate ownership across the full assessment universe (not company-specific, to prevent gaming). A pre-announced rising trajectory converts $\tau_h$ into a pre-committed cost that ownership structures must plan against, which is itself a deterrence input. The transitional deterrence gap — during the ramp period, opacity may remain cheaper than individual WDT assessment for some positions at the lower initial $\tau_h$ — is accepted, provided the ramp window is short enough (three to five years) that the gap cannot be exploited with confidence across a multi-year holding period. A **joint-calibration constraint** is established: the $\tau_h$ ramp cannot be calibrated in isolation from the displacement of CIT and dividend taxation, because a rising $\tau_h$ combined with non-matching CIT/dividend reductions creates a wedge advantaging opacity as a hedge. The ramp must be co-designed with the CIT and dividend displacement schedule as a single joint trajectory. The Governing Council's factional structure — TP members from transparent-ownership industries favouring fast progression, TP members from attribution-hard industries having incentive to reveal attribution feasibility accurately, FS balancing with fiscal concerns, DR evaluating without a stake — is identified as epistemically superior to technocratic calibration at a single point. Three additional Governing Council calibration parameters follow: ramp window length, step-trigger parameters, and the joint-calibration requirement as a constraint on how the Council exercises its authority.

CORP.A v2.0 completes the §F analysis with two new sections. **§F.8** states the general principle derived from the entity-type analysis: conventional tax avoidance is a legal-category game whose profitability depends on gaps between differently-rated or differently-timed tax bases; the WDT removes most of those gaps by asking where the wealth went rather than what legal form was used. The conditions required to defeat the WDT through structural means are mutually incompatible: durable benefit under effective control produces an economic claim; a claim held through another entity resolves through attribution or bears $\tau_m$; an undervalued asset creates a valuation problem (deferred, not eliminated); genuinely transferred wealth leaves the taxpayer poorer. The residual is narrower than under existing systems: valuation accuracy at the top of the distribution remains a permanent challenge, and the Route D entry basis is the genuine structural residual, but the structural conditions under which conventional avoidance works are changed more fundamentally than is commonly assumed. **§F.9** addresses **market manipulation**. A short position is a bilateral claim between counterparties: the reference company's structural fate does not affect the short seller's gain, which runs against the counterparty and is measured across assessment dates regardless of what subsequently happens to the company. The "short → destroy → resurrect" strategy achieves nothing. The reverse attack — artificially inflating a target's asset before assessment to force their WDT liability higher — is self-correcting: the target recognises a positive delta and pays; when the manipulation reverses, the target receives a proportional refund; the attack creates a timing cost, not a permanent wedge; the manipulator's own gain is taxed through their own assessment. Assessment-date gaming through coordinated brief price movement is bounded by the same constraints as the sell-and-repurchase gaming already noted in CORP §5.10 (trade scale, gap length, carrying cost) and is accepted as an imperfection present in any annual measurement system.

## 7. The Constitutional Governance Paper (GOV), Appendix (GOV.A), and Operational Appendix (GOV.B)

GOV designs the institutional architecture the WDT requires, derived from the mechanism's own transactions rather than from inherited assumptions about how such institutions typically look. The standard applied throughout is comparative rather than absolute: harder to capture than the alternatives, more visible when capture is attempted, and leaving more worth inheriting if it happens anyway. Operational detail for all mechanisms described in GOV — chamber mechanics, appointment processes, voting arithmetic, SWF operational specification, Route D auction conduct rules — is in GOV.B.

Every proposed feature is tested against a five-point mechanism-shaped standard: it still works with the enforcer deleted; cost and act are the same transaction; cost is proportional to the size of the act; cost is in a currency the specific actor cannot discount; and no actor defines the inputs that determine its own cost.

A sixth architectural commitment is named explicitly in GOV §2.1 (added v2.3): the no-monopoly principle. No WDT body should hold a monopoly on any input the mechanism requires, including data. This extends the mechanism-shaped test into a named structural constraint on institutional design: wherever a single body's exclusive control over an input would allow that body to define its own cost or verification standard, that monopoly must be broken. The principle has direct bearing on the Administrator's data architecture — the credential-issuance model in GOV.B §B.4.6 is its operational expression.

The corrected derivation (GOV §3; full transaction-by-transaction comparison with the failed three-estate first attempt in GOV.A §C) reads the mechanism's verbs — delta measurement, tax flow, refund flow, asset valuation, Route D auction trigger, surplus allocation — rather than assuming a body for each inherited role. This produces four acting positions plus one flagged endpoint: the Taxpayer, the Valuer, the auction-trigger confirmation function, the Allocator, and Dividend Recipients as an endpoint. "Government" does not survive as a single entity. The three-body Valuation Body architecture in GOV §6.1 is the settled instantiation of two lever-positions the derivation identified (Valuer and independent auction-trigger confirmation), not three; why three bodies rather than two is explained in GOV §6.1 and GOV.A §C.

Three chambers hold political legitimacy in the Governing Council, derived from the mechanism's own transactions and from the anti-collusion guarantee. The Taxpayer Chamber (TP) holds 25% of total vote share, rebalancing against FS; membership tracks WDT eligibility automatically. The Fiscal Sovereign Chamber (FS) holds 25%, rebalancing against TP; membership is tied to constitutional office. The Dividend Recipient Chamber (DR) holds 50%, fixed permanently; this share is derived from the anti-collusion guarantee (TP and FS's unanimous opposition must be independently sufficient to defeat any joint TP/FS proposal) and is an enumerated structural clause rather than a calibration parameter. DR is filled by monthly birth-month lottery with staggered one-year terms and holds no proposing right. A mathematical property of the current 50/25/25 allocation — derived in GOV.B §C.1 — is that at T = 50 the nay condition is automatically satisfied whenever the yay-majority condition holds; the two conditions are not independent at this threshold, and lowering DR's share below 50% would change the fundamental constitutional character of the voting system, not merely weaken the guarantee.

A proposal passes under the dual-threshold rule only if nays stay below DR's vote share and yays exceed 50% of votes actually cast, with non-votes excluded from the denominator. Any single DR member may trigger a Tier 2 review at any time by burning their seat, immediately and permanently. Structural proposals touching the enumerated clause list trigger Tier 2 automatically. Withdrawal is free before a proposal's first conclusion; rebalancing cost attaches on conclusion.

Four categories of executive body carry out the mechanism's transactions without holding Governing Council votes: three independent Valuation Bodies under identical mandates (flagging body identified and excluded; the other two produce sealed estimates opened simultaneously; unanimous corroboration triggers the auction notice); the Allocator (single person recommending surplus distribution across general government revenue, directed labour relief, and reinvestment; named the most capture-vulnerable body in the architecture — a description of a structural feature, not a design flaw, since the role requires inside connections to both TP and FS to perform the synthesis function; appointed by T1 vote after proposal by either FS or TP; serves without a term limit; removable by T2 vote with the rebalancing cost falling on the proposing chamber if removal succeeds, and no cost to any chamber if T2 fails to remove; may resign at any point including between a seat-burn and the resulting T2 vote); the SWF Custodian (long-tenure financial institution, Bank of England analogue in the UK, pre-funding the refund liability under a hard solvency floor with genuine bounded discretion above it); and the Administrator (no vote, no discretion, transmission only, fixed publication cycle, format set externally). The SWF Custodian is the one executive body stated plainly as a design choice rather than derived from the lever test. Appointment mechanics, tenure, operational constraints, and independence requirements for all four body types are in GOV.B §B.

The Allocator's design was revised in GOV v2.7. The prior framing treated capture as a vulnerability to be mitigated through a cooling-off bar, independence criteria, and TP exclusion from appointment. The revised design treats capture as structural and designed-in: the Allocator must be embedded in both TP's and FS's epistemic worlds to perform the synthesis the Governing Council needs. An Allocator who cannot speak candidly with TP members about genuine attribution constraints, and with FS members about genuine fiscal timing pressures, cannot produce recommendations that reflect private knowledge the published data does not contain. The inside connections are the mechanism through which the role functions, not a corruption of it. The mandate is correspondingly broadened from narrow-technical to explicitly broad-advisory, covering economics, geopolitics, fiscal timing, and the cultural and political context bearing on what form of relief serves the terminal goal at any given moment. The appointment structure changes from FS-appointed, DR-confirmed to: either FS or TP proposes a candidate; a T1 vote across all three chambers confirms; the proposing chamber's endorsement is recorded and bears the rebalancing cost if the Allocator is subsequently removed on T2. The cooling-off bar is removed: it was designed to prevent the very relational capital the role requires. Long tenure under this structure is a sign of performance rather than entrenchment — an Allocator who consistently produces reasoning DR finds credible will face seat-burn challenges that fail, which strengthens the Allocator's position without costing the challenging chamber anything, while a successful removal costs the proposing chamber rebalancing share. The popularity test — whether DR finds the published reasoning credible — is the correct measure of the role's performance. Full revised operational specification is in GOV.B §B.2; GOV.A §B.2–B.3 carries the revised instrument audit.

GOV §6.4 (extended in v2.3) provides the definitive characterisation of the Administrator's function. The Administrator is a credential issuer and consistency confirmer, not a truth-discoverer. It issues verifiable credentials per assessment year confirming that a taxpayer's submission is internally consistent and arithmetically correct relative to the prior year's accepted values; it does not independently verify the truth of declared values, which is the Valuation Bodies' function. This characterisation carries a compliance argument for data minimisation: the minimum-necessary-information principle follows from the mechanism's own design rather than from privacy values alone. The Administrator needs only what is required to issue a consistency credential — prior accepted values, current submission, and assessment window election — and can issue that credential without holding a comprehensive picture of a taxpayer's portfolio. This makes the Administrator's limited data footprint a structural feature of what it is, not a policy concession. The operational implementation of this architecture is in GOV.B §B.4.6.

Ten enumerated structural clauses define the properties the system must preserve to remain the same kind of tax. Proposals touching them trigger automatic Tier 2 and a permanent rebalancing cost. The ten clauses protect: the delta tax base; refund symmetry; the lifetime contribution envelope; the SWF's existence and sole capitalisation purpose; closure of the attribution gap; commitment of net WDT revenue above pre-existing obligations to labour and consumption tax relief; the individual as the unit of taxation; the non-discretionary Route D auction mechanism with at least three independent Valuation Bodies; DR's anti-collusion guarantee vote share; and a permanent, public, and undiscretionary record of all Governing Council decisions, vote outcomes, and valuation data (the publishable-output list, added as clause 10 in GOV v2.4, closing cross-paper register item #33). The enumerated list is itself on the list. Seven clauses follow directly from the derivation or the foundational axioms of WP and MF; clauses eight, nine, and ten rest partly on judgment, which is stated plainly in GOV §5.2.

The Route D auction mechanism architecture (GOV §6.1; full operational process in GOV.B §G). Three independent Valuation Bodies operate under identical mandates: a flagging body identifies an outlier and is excluded from what follows; the other two bodies produce sealed independent estimates opened simultaneously; when both non-flagging bodies unanimously confirm the declared value falls outside the trigger threshold, the Administrator publishes an auction notice. The asset is offered at the taxpayer's own declared price; only third parties may bid; the taxpayer holds a right of first refusal at the highest third-party bid price within a defined window after the auction closes. The winning bid price replaces the declared value as the new recognised basis. Proceeds go to the taxpayer in all cases; the state's interest is collected through the taxpayer's individual WDT assessment in the auction year. The taxpayer exclusion from bidding (and right of first refusal as the alternative) is settled architecture as of GOV v2.1.

The classification veto mechanism provides the primary non-discretionary route for reclassifying proposals as structural. Any voter may simultaneously attach a Tier 2 classification veto label to their substantive vote at no additional cost. A simple majority of votes cast carrying the label triggers reclassification to Tier 2, with the rebalancing cost attaching on conclusion. Label counts are published by the Administrator in real time alongside vote tallies. The statistical distribution of label activity across all proposals over time is part of the permanent public record, providing a revealed baseline against which unusual label concentration on a specific proposal is legible without qualitative judgment. The DR seat-burn remains available as a targeted escalation tool, now informed by the visible label distribution rather than operating blind. Classification defaults to self-declaration by the proposing chamber; confirmed misclassification following a DR seat-burn challenge results in retroactive rebalancing cost from the original proposal date.

DR members have access to an Administrator-run internal forum: member-post-only, fully public to view, access verified against lottery selection records. A separate fully public forum is available to any person. Neither forum is mandatory; informal communication outside them remains free. TP's internal factionalism is treated as both inevitable and healthy; the architecture's response to TP's collective wealth concentration is structural rather than deliberative. FS operates within existing governmental culture and accountability structures; the WDT does not regulate FS's internal process.

The taxpayer history record is a mandatory Administrator output: each taxpayer's longitudinal participation record comprising taxes paid, refunds received, lifetime envelope balance, and assessment window elections over time. It is subject to periodic deposit at designated archival institutions with independent preservation mandates; the British Library is the reference institution for the UK jurisdiction. Distributed archiving protects the record against the slow degradation the Administrator's own mandate cannot fully reach.

The exit bridging facility operates on a fully symmetric bond structure. Where the expected exit delta is positive, the taxpayer posts a bond proportional to the estimated liability before departure; the Custodian holds it as secured collateral. Where the expected delta is negative, the SWF posts a bond to the taxpayer as security for the expected refund before departure. Where direction is uncertain, both sides post proportional bonds; bonds net on settlement. Bond release on a negative delta is in full plus any refund owed. Bond sizing ratios on both sides are Governing Council parameters calibrated against Phase One exit data. The symmetric bond structure is the state accepting downside exposure at exit in the same way the symmetric refund mechanism accepts it during the assessment period. The Custodian's mandate explicitly covers the bridging facility as a distinct exposure category subject to the same solvency floor as the refund liability. Full mandate, bond-sizing principles, and operational sequence are in GOV.B §E.3.

Mode B governance failure — the state honouring the WDT's mechanics while abandoning what the mechanics exist to serve — is introduced in GOV §4 as the motivating illustration for the structural safeguards. It has two forms. The discrete form (outright revenue diversion) is substantially closed by enumerated clause 6 and the automatic rebalancing trigger it carries. The drift form (valuation methodology loosening gradually) is acknowledged as irreducible and addressed through residue mechanisms.

Governance decay has four sub-forms: definitional drift, procedural calcification, constituency dissolution, and role-fidelity drift. Three are irreducible. The constituency dissolution mechanism is the one tractable sub-form: DR's volunteer rate is a byproduct number rather than a fabricable record, and the mechanism expands the lottery draw count when the rate falls and decays it back asymmetrically on recovery. For the three irreducible sub-forms, the honest response is residue — the Public Valuation Register, the SWF's actuarial record, the permanent published decision archive — durable assets that survive a captured period and give a future legitimate effort something to rebuild from. The full four-sub-form analysis is in GOV.A §E. Mode B's discrete and drift forms are treated in GOV §4 and GOV.A §E respectively; the state/taxpayer relational framing (reciprocal partnership) remains settled per GOV.A §E (previously §E.2) and MF §7.

GOV.A (v2.1) is the intellectual appendix: §A = three failure-mode taxonomy (oracle failure, self-referential power, resource-defines-truth degeneration) with real-world instances; §B = audit of existing WDT instruments against the five-point mechanism-shaped test; §C = rejected first derivation — full transaction-by-transaction comparison with the corrected derivation; §D = explored and dropped mechanisms, with the objection recorded against each; §E = governance decay four sub-forms only (Mode B content dissolved into GOV §4). §B.2 updated in v2.1: the Allocator's T1/T2 appointment and removal structure assessed as closer to mechanism-shaped than prior framing acknowledged; capture-as-feature reframing changes the instrument-audit test from 'is the Allocator independent?' to 'does the published reasoning make synthesis quality legible to DR?'; §B.3 audit summary updated accordingly.

GOV.B (v0.5) is the operational appendix: full chamber specifications for TP, FS, and DR (including the constituency dissolution mechanism trigger logic, the DR forum access verification, and Phase Two DR scale problem); full executive body operational detail (Valuation Body appointment, staggered terms, hard institutional separation, and removal criteria; Allocator appointment mechanics (either-chamber proposal, T1 confirmation, endorsing-chamber rebalancing cost on successful T2 removal), publication requirements, and Allocator-as-public-figure section; SWF Custodian statutory mandate extension process; Administrator format-consistency requirement and mandatory output list); voting mechanics in full (dual-threshold worked arithmetic including T = 50 property, Tier 1 schedule, Tier 2 three-case timing, classification veto label mechanics, withdrawal routes, missed Tier 2 consequences by chamber); rebalancing conservation arithmetic and self-policing conditions; SWF operational detail (solvency floor automatic-consequence principle, drawdown condition pre-crisis commitment cycle, bridging facility bond-posting sequence and settlement, unit-holder rights and governance activation threshold, annual stewardship statement mandatory content, and UK institutional mapping for Custodian mandate extension); per-actor cost mechanisms (vote-share rebalancing for TP/FS, Public Valuation Register disclosure on proposal entry, ballot linkage for diffuse citizens, solvency-ratio collapse of future-generations interest, and visibility/cost distinction); and Route D auction process in full (sealed-estimate protocol and non-anchoring requirement, unanimity requirement rationale, auction conduct rules including marketing period, bidding rules, no-bid case, basis-reset documentation, assessment-year delta calculation, published record three-layer structure, and administrative fee schedule).

Three sections were added in v0.2: the credential-issuance data architecture model (§B.4.6), the privacy election mechanism (§B.4.7), and the Custodian inflationary rotation mandate (§E.7). Their substance is unchanged and is stated in the paragraphs below. GOV.B v0.4 added §H: the corporate equity settlement facility mandate extension, specifying two new Custodian exposure categories (secured corporate lending and a distinct corporate equity portfolio), stewardship statement requirements for the facility, its relationship to the existing mandate architecture, and five Governing Council calibration parameters (pre-assessment volume-weighted average window; loan interest rate; minimum annual repayment schedule; margin call threshold; maximum holding period before mandatory sale). GOV.B v0.5 revised §B.2 (Allocator) throughout to implement the GOV v2.7 redesign; see the Allocator redesign paragraph above for substance.

First, the credential-issuance data architecture model (§B.4.6). The Administrator issues a verifiable credential per assessment year to each taxpayer; the credential stack accumulates across years in the taxpayer's own custody rather than in a centralised Administrator repository. Selective disclosure follows from this architecture: a taxpayer presenting a credential to a verifier can prove consistency of a specific assessment year's submission without disclosing others. Zero-knowledge proof tooling is named as an available extension, not a required component. The verifier-learns-minimum principle is an architectural commitment that follows from the no-monopoly principle in GOV §2.1 and the credential-issuer characterisation in GOV §6.4: verifiers should learn only what is necessary to confirm the relevant consistency claim, and the architecture is designed to enforce this without relying on Administrator discretion.

Second, the privacy election mechanism (§B.4.7). At each annual submission, taxpayers tag each asset as disclosed or private. Disclosed assets attract a rate discount relative to the standard rate; private assets attract a rate premium. The framing is two equivalent participation modes — the mechanism functions identically under either election — not a compliance vs. non-compliance distinction. Non-fungible assets require a whole-asset election: an asset cannot be partially disclosed. The rate differential coefficient is a single Governing Council calibration parameter under the Tier 1 process; the paper specifies the constraint that the expected revenue under the two modes must be equivalent in expectation, which determines the relationship between the discount and premium rather than their absolute levels. This section operationalises the privacy-election concept introduced in BEHAV §6.4 and provides its mechanism-level design.

Third, the Custodian inflationary rotation mandate (§E.7). GOV.B §E.7 specifies that the Custodian's statutory mandate should carry defined parameters for accelerated Route C equity rotation under inflationary trigger conditions. Two parameters are identified as Governing Council calibration items to be specified in the mandate: the inflationary trigger threshold (the rate of sustained price-level increase that activates accelerated rotation) and the accelerated holding period (the reduced minimum hold duration for Route C positions during the activation window). ENV §7 had identified accelerated Route C rotation as an automatic countercyclical instrument; GOV.B §E.7 converts that identification into a named mandate specification, so that the countercyclical effect operates as deliberate parameterised policy rather than an emergent consequence of the mandate's existing structure.
