## 8. The Rates and Revenue Paper (RATES) and Appendix (RATES.A)

RATES answers the arithmetic question: can a progressive tax on annual wealth deltas, calibrated to UK data, fund modern government at a scale sufficient to displace the existing tax base at individual burdens that remain proportionate? The answer is yes, without qualification. The companion Appendix (RATES.A) provides the full model specification (§A) and model output (§B); it is cited throughout as [RATES.A].

**The two models.** The paper uses two models in sequence. The SWF Solvency Model (SSM) applies actual historical UK equity returns uniformly across the entire taxable population — the worst-case correlated-shock assumption, maximising simultaneous refund pressure and minimising net income — as the nominal UK budget grows at 4.51% per annum (corrected in v2.6; derived from 1999–2019 TME data, per JUR §2.11). Its primary output is the LRR breakeven year: the first year the LRR balance reaches the recommended capitalisation floor of 3 years of government expenditure, the point at which fiscal replacement is viable. The Taxpayer Cohort Model (TCM) is calibrated to the LRR breakeven year produced by the SSM, applying four persistent heterogeneous growth tier differentials (ranging from −4.55pp to +3.45pp relative to the historical mean of 10.45%) to the same rotated historical return sequence. The two models share all parameters and return data, differing only in their distributional assumption; together they bracket the plausible revenue range. The full specification of both models — inputs, mechanics, and reproducibility instructions — is in RATES.A §A.

**Reference scenario.** The paper's reference scenario throughout is the 2007 Balanced start year at Balanced parameters ($\tau_0$ = 15%, $\tau_m$ = 70%, k = 0.001 per £m, W_min = £2m). Under the UK equity return data used and at the corrected budget growth rate of 4.51% p.a. (derived from UK TME 1999–00 to 2019–20, per JUR §2.11), 2007 produces the longest LRR fill time of all 73 viable start years (29 years), making it the hardest illustrative case in the dataset on the transition-speed dimension. The choice of worst-case reference is deliberate: it provides the most conservative baseline for the revenue and burden claims. All figures in the paper are illustrative of the mechanism's behaviour under one historical record, not predictions of future performance.

**Individual burden.** The maximum annual wealth burden across the entire modelled population at the 2007 Balanced reference is 0.75% of net worth per year, requiring simultaneous membership of the top 0.01% wealth bracket and the highest persistent-outperformance growth tier across the full 29-year horizon. The maximum effective rate on gains is 22.4%, at the very top of both distributions simultaneously, as a lifetime average over a 29-year horizon including loss years with refunds. For most taxpayers the annual burden is a fraction of a percent of existing wealth, because the tax base is the annual increment and the symmetric refund mechanism offsets loss years against gain years across the horizon.

**Revenue claim.** The central revenue claim is directional and order-of-magnitude: the WDT raises revenue in the appreciable tens of percent of UK government expenditure during the capitalisation window (SRR fill to LRR fill). Two coverage ratios bracket the plausible range. The SSM coverage ratio (average annual net SSM income over the capitalisation window divided by average annual expenditure over the same window) is 21.3% for the 2007 reference, reflecting the correlated-shock floor. The TCM coverage ratio, computed on the same basis using heterogeneous tier differentials, is 27.7%. The gap between them at the lower floor rate is narrower than at prior calibrations, reflecting that lower τ₀ reduces the premium that heterogeneous tier compounding produces over the correlated-shock floor; neither ratio is more correct than the other. A known boundary-alignment limitation means the two ratios are not computed over precisely identical year sets; both should be read as order-of-magnitude indicators. The full specification is in RATES.A §A.6. Total average annual TCM revenue at the 2007 Balanced reference is approximately £673.1b over the full horizon (£640.7b during the capitalisation window average).

**Historical starting-year sensitivity.** The SSM was run at Balanced parameters from every viable start year in the 1947–2019 UK equity return data (73 start years). The headline result is a 100% success rate across all 73 start years and all four economic cycles (post-war growth 1947–59; long boom 1960–79; liberalisation 1980–99; crisis decade 2000–19). Success is defined precisely: the LRR fills within the 71-year modelling window, and either the SRR never breaches or, if it does, the LRR balance at the moment of first SRR breach is sufficient to cover the SRR deficit in full. The SRR fill year is invariant at 3 across all 73 start years. The LRR breakeven ranges from 7 to 29 years (median 13). The TCM coverage ratio ranges from 24.0% (2003 start) to 134.5% (1974 start), with a median of 40.3%. The full 73-row sweep table and statistical pass are in RATES.A §B.4 and §B.5. The budget growth rate used throughout is 4.51% p.a. (corrected from 5.24% in v2.6; derivation in JUR §2.11).

**SWF reserves and milestones.** The SWF comprises two internal reserves on distinct timescales. The SWF Refund Reserve (SRR) is ring-fenced for the refund liability only; the SSM-derived working capitalisation ratio is 2.77× net annual WDT income, with a recommended Governing Council floor of 3×. The Labour Relief Reserve (LRR) funds the transition account, with a recommended floor of 3 years of government expenditure. SRR fill (invariant at year 3 across all 73 start years) makes the refund guarantee mechanically credible. LRR fill (7–29 years, median 13) makes full Phase Two viable. At the 2007 Balanced reference, annual expenditure at LRR breakeven is £3,980b; the SRR balance at that point is £1,498b; the LRR surplus is £1,041b. The capitalisation window spans years 3–29 (25 years). These are economic events; Phase One and Phase Two are political operating postures the Governing Council controls, not labels for the intervals between milestones.

Once the LRR reaches its floor target, continued accumulation is in tension with enumerated clauses 4 and 6 of GOV §7.2: clause 4 restricts the SWF's capitalisation purpose to pre-funding the refund liability, and clause 6 requires net revenue above pre-existing obligations to be directed toward labour and consumption tax relief. Post-LRR-fill rate recalibration is therefore architecturally required, not optional housekeeping.

**Design positions settled.** Two design positions were settled by RATES and remain fully in force. Full symmetry of the loss-refund mechanism is adopted: partial symmetry breaks the Domar-Musgrave risk-sharing logic mechanically and would abandon the state's downside commitment foundationally. The assessment window premium is excluded from the reference revenue model as a Phase One calibration question, demonstrating the mechanism functions without it. A third position on corporate rate-floor calibration was initially recorded in RATES Appendix C.3 but has since been superseded by the CORP.A disaggregation of $\tau_prov$ and $\tau_h$ as distinct optimisation problems; RATES Appendix C.3 carries a supersession notice and CORP.A §B.1–B.2 contain the revised framework. Appendix C was absorbed into §4 of the current version; Appendix D (historical sensitivity full results) was retired and its contents moved to RATES.A.

**Pre-behavioural baseline.** The revenue estimates are explicitly pre-behavioural. Behavioural responses — migration, restructuring, and avoidance — will reduce actual revenue by an amount that only Phase One implementation can establish. This is the principal source of overstatement in the reference figures. BEHAV (§9a below) sets out the design framework within which Phase One can generate evidence on these questions; it does not itself resolve them.

---

## 9. The Parameter Space and Governing Council Calibration Paper (SWEEPS) and Appendix (SWEEPS.A)

SWEEPS is a calibration reference paper. It does not design or modify any WDT mechanism. Its subject is the parameter space the Governing Council inherits: what the four rate-function parameters actually control, how they interact across the two sweep datasets, and what the Council is calibrating when it moves each lever.

The paper draws on two complementary datasets. VAL.S examines how the four rate-function parameters (τ₀, τ_m, k, W_min) affect declaration incentive properties: the tolerant zone width, the N-crossing threshold for aggressive overstaters, and the understater penalty plateau ceiling. RATES.S examines how the same parameters affect fiscal outcomes: TCM coverage ratios and LRR fill year across the 73-year historical start-year sweep. Neither dataset recommends values.

The central finding is parameter separability: the four parameters are doing largely independent jobs across the two dimensions. τ₀ governs entry-rate signalling and overstater self-correction timing (primary fiscal lever at canonical k). τ_m governs tail deterrence for egregious understaters and is fiscally inert for the current modelled population — the clearest instance of complete separability in the sweep. k governs the progressivity of the rate schedule and the width of the tolerant zone; its fiscal consequence is limited within the 100%-success region (k ≤ 0.01) but the success rate falls to 96% at k = 0.05 and 90% at k = 0.1, which bounds how far k can be raised without compromising solvency guarantees. W_min governs the scope of the mechanism (who is subject to it) and has near-zero leverage on declaration incentive properties for taxpayers already above the threshold.

The one genuine cross-dataset tension is τ₀. Higher τ₀ accelerates fiscal capitalisation and shortens the LRR fill period; lower τ₀ preserves and strengthens the self-limiting correction for aggressive overstaters. The crossing disappears entirely for α = 2.0 above approximately τ₀ = 29–32% within realistic holding horizons (Table A.6). There is no setting that simultaneously optimises both: this is the most consequential single calibration the Council faces, and the τ₀ × W_min joint surface (not yet generated) is the minimum further work required to characterise it quantitatively.

Reserve multiplier sweeps (SWEEPS.A §§B.6–B.7) confirm 100% success across all tested srr_ratio (1× to 10×) and lrr_years (0.5 to 8 years) values across all 73 historical start years. The 3× srr_ratio floor is confirmed as appropriately placed: the 2006 scenario first shows a covered SRR breach below 2.5× and no breach from 2.5× onward. The 3× lrr_years floor gives the RATES reference median fill of 13 years (at corrected 4.51% budget growth). At 4.51%, the k sweep achieves 100% success throughout the full k range tested; the 96%/90% deterioration at k = 0.05/0.1 noted in SWEEPS v0.1 was an artefact of the prior 5.24% budget growth rate and does not apply at the corrected value. The residual — empirical confirmation of solvency behaviour under an actual downturn — is a Phase One item.

The paper establishes a secondary finding on canonical parameter origin: in SWEEPS v0.3 figures, the N = 29 reference line is the canonical VAL.S LRR fill year at τ₀ = 15% and the corrected budget growth rate of 4.51%. Earlier SWEEPS versions carried N = 34 (from the prior RATES Balanced scenario at τ₀ = 20%) and N = 32 (from the intermediate parameter pass); both have been corrected to N = 29 throughout.

The three-chamber structure generates appropriate disagreement on every rate-function parameter, with no single chamber or faction able to drive any lever to its logical extreme. The small lever set is framed as a democratic good: calibration decisions whose consequences can be characterised in advance, stated publicly, and evaluated against outcomes.

Two open questions are generated: SWEEPS-1 (revenue frontier — whether a parameter combination dominates on both dimensions simultaneously, or the τ₀ tension produces an irreducible frontier; assigned to RATES.A extension) and SWEEPS-2 (Custodian mandate SRR buffer condition for drawdown acceleration; conditional on Phase One data; amendment, if warranted, in GOV.B). SWEEPS-3 (reserve multiplier sweep) is closed within the paper itself. The canonical LRR fill range across the historical sweep is 7–29 years (median 13) at corrected 4.51% budget growth.

---

## 10. The Behavioural Robustness Paper (BEHAV)

BEHAV is a companion paper (v1.4, 14 August 2026 — full structural rewrite; §6.3, §8.12, §8.13, §10 added; §9.2 substantially rewritten; §§10–12 renumbered §§11–13).

BEHAV addresses behavioural failure: the tendency of tax systems to function only under the behavioural assumptions built into their design, collapsing when taxpayers respond differently. Its central claim is that behavioural robustness — the degree to which a mechanism's effectiveness is independent of any particular assumption about how taxpayers will behave — is a design property that can be derived and argued from first principles, without requiring behavioural predictions the empirical record cannot support.

The paper's primary structural contributions are: a taxonomy of five friction types that drive the most damaging behavioural responses to taxation regardless of the headline rate (information friction / complexity; visibility friction / opacity; legitimacy friction / perceived unfairness; feedback friction / delay; compliance friction / administrative burden); five design principles derived from that taxonomy (Clarity, Reciprocity, Fairness, Responsiveness, Accessibility); the concept of The Membrane — the layer of procedures, communications, defaults, and feedback loops through which taxpayers experience the institution, distinct from the mechanism itself; and a nine-shape taxonomy of behavioural responses (Shape 1 full cooperative compliance through Shape 9 active resistance) against which robustness is evaluated. Six specific administrative-layer interventions are proposed: an annual entitlement statement making refund entitlement visible in real time; provisional refund notification in loss years; an asset classification register with safe harbour; a legible SWF annual number for public visibility; a default-long assessment window election; and a taxpayer history record showing longitudinal participation.

Three positions established in v1.1 remain fully in force. First, the enforcement paradigm shift (§8.11): the WDT's enforcement posture is passive collection rather than active detection. The standard hiding strategies — unattributed corporate structures (taxed at $\tau_h$ by default; establishing standing to contest $\tau_h$ is itself an attribution event), illegal off-books concealment (self-punishing through compounding crystallisation risk), realisation to cash (recorded delta; lifetime envelope preserves history), hard cash off-books (existing criminal law) — are all either self-defeating or self-punishing under the mechanism's own architecture. The genuine residual is Route D entry basis manipulation, which is narrower, more visible, and more tractable than conventional hiding. Second, the Administrator-as-consistency-confirmer principle (§7.5): the Administrator's verification task is arithmetic confirmation rather than truth-discovery; the minimum-necessary-information principle follows from the mechanism's own design rather than from privacy values alone. Third, full privacy compatibility as a membrane property (§6.5): a privacy election is a choice between two equivalent participation modes, not a concession to taxpayer preferences or a compromise of mechanism integrity.

Four further positions are established in v1.4.

**The interaction structure of membrane health dimensions (§6.3).** The five membrane health dimensions are not independent. All ten pairwise relationships are mapped. The most important relationships: Clarity and Accessibility share the strongest complementarity — the four-route architecture reduces Information friction and Compliance friction in the same move; Reciprocity and Fairness are the most easily misread — a system delivering symmetric economics but perceived as administered inconsistently satisfies Reciprocity and fails Fairness simultaneously, which is the WDT's most acute Phase One vulnerability; Responsiveness and Accessibility compete directly for administrative resource, requiring sequential rather than parallel prioritisation. Fairness occupies a distinctive structural position: it is downstream of all four other dimensions and also degrades independently through arbitrary administrative discretion that none of the other dimensions can address. Fairness degradation should be treated as a leading indicator of membrane failure rather than a lagging consequence.

**The route distribution of WDT-taxable wealth (§8.12) and its structural implications (§8.13).** The enforcement residual identified in §8.11 scales directly with the share of WDT-taxable wealth that classifies as Route D. Directional estimates, acknowledging the WAS undersampling caveat above £3m identified in JUR §2.4: Route A (listed equities, bonds, pensions, cash) 40–55%; Route B (property, agricultural land, illiquid alternatives with professional valuation) 20–30%; Route C (self-declared fungibles) 5–10%; Route D (private company equity, illiquid non-fungibles, collectibles) 10–20%. Three structural features constrain Route D's share below what the universe of non-fungible assets might suggest: most large UK private companies eventually list (transitioning from Route D to Route A at IPO); the corporate delta levy covers listed companies separately; and the compounding cost of understatement established in VAL pushes Route D-eligible assets toward Route B adoption where a credible professional appraisal is possible. Route D at 10–20% means the enforcement residual applies to a minority of WDT-taxable wealth by volume. Two caveats are stated plainly. First, Route D concentration is heavily skewed toward the very top of the WDT population: a route covering 10–20% of aggregate WDT-taxable wealth may cover 40–50% of the liability attributable to the top 500 taxpayers. Volume share and revenue share are not the same number. Second, the boundary between Route B and Route D is partly a taxpayer election; Phase One route adoption data is the primary correction mechanism for these estimates. The bias toward Routes A and B is structurally positive for three reasons beyond reduced Route D exposure: the self-correction mechanisms are strongest in A and B (the entry basis problem that generates Route D's enforcement residual does not exist there); the delta self-correction operates most cleanly where values are independently verifiable; and A and B dominance makes revenue more forecastable, which matters for SRR capitalisation and Governing Council planning.

**The cross-base fiscal externality — six-part response (§9.2).** The Agrawal, Foremny, and Martinez-Toledano (2025) finding — that wealth-tax-driven migration generates income tax and VAT losses approximately six times the direct revenue loss — is the most serious empirical challenge the paper faces and is stated without softening. Six responses are developed. First, the jurisdictional transfer caveat: the six-to-one ratio is derived from Spanish regional data and is a point estimate from a specific context, not a structural constant; its magnitude in a UK implementation is unknown. Second, the membrane investment multiplier: if the ratio is directionally correct, each departure event prevented by better membrane quality saves not only the direct WDT revenue but approximately six times that amount in preserved cross-base revenue, making membrane quality fiscally urgent rather than merely institutionally desirable. Third, the rate calibration lever: the Governing Council can reduce rates in response to observed departure — a net-positive fiscal move if the resulting retention preserves more cross-base revenue than the rate reduction sacrifices in direct WDT revenue; no prior wealth tax design had this capacity. Fourth, the timeline extension buffer: the Governing Council can extend the SRR and LRR fill windows at the cost of delaying the labour tax relief dividend, trading time for retention without systemic failure. Fifth, the re-entry rule and the externality's temporal shape: because the lifetime contribution envelope travels with a departing taxpayer and is restored on re-entry, the Agrawal externality is front-loaded in Phase One — when the envelope is thin and the mechanism's properties are unproven — and structurally diminishing as the system matures. The externality is a transitional risk concentrated before the mechanism has demonstrated itself, not a permanent structural feature of wealth taxation. Sixth, the immigration possibility, framed as a formal possibility rather than a prediction: the Agrawal finding is derived entirely from conventional wealth taxes sharing a common architecture of asymmetric extraction, no loss participation, and adversarial enforcement. The WDT differs from every wealth tax in the empirical record in three ways directly relevant to a mobile wealth-holder's location calculus — symmetric loss participation, delta base proportional to gain, governance participation through the Taxpayer Chamber. If these features change the rational calculus sufficiently, net inward migration of wealthy individuals is formally possible, which would invert the Agrawal ratio from threat to dividend. This argument is conditional on credible Phase One delivery and is a Phase One empirical question.

**Membrane calcification and the monitoring architecture (§10).** Membrane calcification — the tendency of a mature institution to preserve Membrane processes designed for an earlier taxpayer population — differs structurally from governance decay in that it operates through omission rather than commission. No actor decides to calcify the membrane. GOV's structural mechanisms (enumerated clauses, rebalancing costs) do not transfer directly because they require observable trigger conditions that membrane health lacks. The partial structural response begins with measurement: the five membrane health dimensions each have observable proxies that are byproducts of the Administrator's existing data collection (self-assessment completion rates for Clarity, unprompted refund claim rates for Reciprocity, dispute rates disaggregated by wealth band for Fairness, refund processing times for Responsiveness, professional adviser engagement rates for Accessibility). These should be mandatory Administrator outputs published on a fixed cycle, with Phase One data establishing the baseline. The Taxpayer Chamber is the natural institutional monitor: TP members have direct experiential information about membrane quality that no other body holds, and the one-member-one-vote rule creates a structural hypothesis that the entry-level majority coalition — for whom compliance friction and Reciprocity visibility matter more at the margin than for the ultra-wealthy minority — has both stronger incentive and formal voting power to escalate membrane grievances. The Allocator provides an imperfect but structurally grounded signal for the Fairness dimension specifically: sustained broad-based TP lobbying on membrane quality that saturates the Allocator's published recommendations is a more reliable signal of genuine Fairness degradation than survey data, because it is revealed rather than stated preference and costly to maintain. A motivated TP/DR coalition clears both dual-threshold conditions without FS, providing the structural answer to FS resistance on fiscal grounds. The honest limit: the monitoring architecture requires TP to organise, the Allocator to surface the signal, and DR to prioritise membrane health — reasonable expectations given structural incentive alignment, but expectations rather than guarantees. The mandatory publication cycle for membrane health observables is the membrane equivalent of GOV's residue concept: not a prevention mechanism, but a record that survives if prevention fails.

The emigration objection is addressed through §9.1 and the six-part §9.2. The structural exit closure mechanics — the no-punitive-exit-taxation position, the bridging facility, and the re-entry rule — are developed in CLOSE (§10 below); BEHAV §8.7 and §9.1 cross-reference CLOSE for those.

BEHAV does not model behavioural outcomes, does not predict elasticities, and does not resolve open questions #1, #11, #13, #15, or #17. It sets up the design framework within which Phase One can generate evidence on those questions. Five open questions are generated by BEHAV (BEHAV OQ 1–5), tracked in the register below.

---

## 11. The Position Closure Paper (CLOSE)

CLOSE is a companion paper (v0.2, 24 July 2026).

CLOSE establishes the general theory of WDT position closure: the set of events by which an individual's WDT assessment position ends, and the mechanisms the WDT uses to settle each one. Its central claim is that death, jurisdictional exit, threshold fall-through, and bankruptcy are structurally the same kind of event — the assessment position closes — and that the WDT already possesses, or can straightforwardly derive from existing machinery, a principled settlement procedure for each.

The paper's conceptual contribution is the abstraction itself: shifting from a conventional exit-tax framing — which treats departure as an avoidance act requiring a fiscal deterrent — to a general account of how a delta-based assessment position closes, what the mechanism owes the individual at closure, and what the individual owes the mechanism. The four closure event types share a common settlement sequence: calculate the final delta, honour the symmetric refund if the final delta is negative, settle the running account. Procedural differences follow from the circumstances of each event type; the underlying logic is identical.

Three positions settled in CLOSE are significant across the project. First, the no-punitive-exit-taxation position: the WDT does not impose punitive exit taxation; departure is a legitimate termination event, not an avoidance act requiring coercive response. This follows directly from the cooperative architecture — a punitive exit provision contradicts the foundational reciprocal claim. Second, the bridging facility: for Route D assets at exit closure, the SWF crystallises liability at the declared exit date and allows physical departure before the auction and settlement process completes, decoupling departure from settlement and eliminating the detention problem that conventional exit regimes produce. The symmetric bond structure governing the facility is specified in GOV §8.8: where the expected exit delta is positive the taxpayer posts a bond; where it is negative the SWF posts a bond to the taxpayer as security for the expected refund; where uncertain, both sides post proportional bonds netting on settlement. Third, the re-entry rule: the lifetime contribution envelope is a property of the individual, not the assessment position. It persists across closures and re-entries. A re-entrant carries their prior envelope balance into any new position; the basis is fresh, the envelope history is not. This closes the strategic cycling loophole and — importantly for the emigration objection — provides a structural incentive for long-term participants to return, because their accumulated refund entitlement travels with them.

The symmetric refund obligation persists through closure. If the position closes on a loss, the refund fires at the applicable marginal rate regardless of the closure event type — death, exit, fall-through, or bankruptcy. The cooperative architecture's commitment does not diminish because the individual is dying, departing, or insolvent.

The cross-base fiscal externality (Agrawal et al., 2025) is treated as a Phase One transitional exposure: during Phase One, income tax and VAT losses from WDT-driven departure are not addressed by CLOSE's position closure framework. In Phase Two, where those parallel taxes are displaced by WDT revenue, the externality disappears structurally. CLOSE does not resolve the Phase One exposure; it characterises it honestly and points to the fuller treatment in BEHAV §9.2.

CLOSE's stated limitations: it does not quantify the revenue or behavioural consequences of any closure event type; it does not provide the constitutional and legal analysis of exit and bankruptcy closure in the reference jurisdiction (assigned to JUR); and the Phase Two re-entry rule for foreign nationals with prior WDT-equivalent positions requires bilateral information exchange arrangements that cannot be designed unilaterally. Three open questions remain from CLOSE (CLOSE OQ 2–4), tracked in the register below. CLOSE OQ 1 (SWF Custodian mandate for the exit bridging facility) is closed by GOV v1.4 §8.8 and carries a closure notice in the paper itself as of CLOSE v0.5.

---

## 12. The Political Architecture Paper (POL)

POL is a companion paper (v0.3, 03 August 2026).

POL addresses the question the companion papers left open: whether a wealth tax can survive long enough to work. Its argument is that political durability is a design property, not a political outcome — it can be built in or left out, specified in advance, and evaluated against explicit criteria.

The paper derives three structural failure mechanisms from the empirical record of OECD wealth tax abolition (drawing principally on Perret, 2021, and Bastani and Waldenström, 2020). Mechanism one is legitimacy collapse: a tax perceived as purely extractive, offering no visible reciprocal benefit, loses public support even among non-payers. France's wealth tax carried sixty to eighty percent popular support throughout its final decade and was abolished anyway, because popular endorsement in surveys does not translate into political resistance when the benefit being defended is abstract. Mechanism two is organised opposition advantage: the taxed population is small enough to organise cheaply, wealthy enough to sustain that organisation indefinitely, and influential enough to access decision-makers, media, and advisory networks. The general population has no equivalent per-capita incentive to organise in defence. Mechanism three is institutional brittleness: individually defensible concessions (exemption expansions, threshold drift, enforcement under-resourcing) accumulate into structural hollowing invisible until complete, making formal abolition cheap. Germany's Federal Constitutional Court struck down the wealth tax in 1997 not on economic grounds but because accumulated valuation inconsistencies failed the equal-treatment test. The three mechanisms are mutually reinforcing and produce a characteristic downward spiral; revenue was still flowing at the point of abolition in most cases.

POL then evaluates the WDT's institutions against the three criteria the failure analysis implies (visible reciprocity, organised constituencies with stakes in continuation, and constitutional protection against institutional erosion), and finds that the WDT satisfies all three — not because it was designed against them, but because it was derived from first principles. This redundancy is the paper's central finding: each WDT institution serves multiple functions simultaneously, so the failure of any single political function does not remove the institution carrying it. The symmetric refund exists for Domar-Musgrave, moral, and incentive reasons before it exists for reciprocity reasons; the SWF exists for pre-funding reasons before it exists for constituency-building reasons; the labour dividend exists for the terminal goal and GOV §7.2 clause 6 reasons before it exists for organised counter-interest reasons; the enumerated clauses protect mechanism integrity before they protect against institutional erosion. An opponent must pay multiple independent costs to remove any single feature.

The paper also addresses the credibility bootstrapping problem in detail: the WDT's cooperative architecture only becomes credible by operating, which requires participants to have already cooperated. Phase One is the period of maximum exposure and minimum institutional redundancy. The paper identifies partial mitigations (partial SRR capitalisation creates friction around unwinding even pre-fill; a voluntary high-profile Phase One cohort changes the optics of dismantling; a completed refund cycle before a hostile government arrives partially demonstrates the commitment) without claiming they are sufficient. The honest conclusion is that Phase One vulnerability is irreducible by design; the design objective is to move through the bootstrapping period as quickly as the political atmosphere allows.

The self-shaping problem is named in §7 and developed in Appendix A: the WDT's institutions change the political interests of the people inside them, creating new constituencies and conflicts as a consequence of operating, including visible institutional tiers the mechanism never intended but cannot prevent. The paper addresses the tiered citizenship risk directly, argues that the WDT does not introduce tiers to an egalitarian society but makes existing invisible, unobligated tiers visible and obligated, and names the feudal comparison in order to explain why the structural distance from feudalism follows from getting the mechanism right rather than from trying to avoid the comparison. The ultimate wager — that visible, obligated, democratically constrained tiers are more manageable than invisible, unobligated, democratically unconstrained ones — is stated plainly as a wager rather than an established claim.

Four open questions are generated by POL (POL-1 through POL-4), tracked in the register below. The paper also inherits by cross-reference items #11, #37, #38, and BEHAV-1, whose resolution conditions are unaffected by POL but whose political significance POL clarifies.

---

## 13. The Phase One Paper (PHASE1)

Phase One is a boundary paper. Its central claim is that the WDT's design is complete and internally consistent, and that the following questions are genuine empirical unknowns that only a live system can resolve — not gaps in the design. It closes the series honestly rather than leaving it open-ended.

The paper identifies seven empirical clusters: behavioural response to the cooperative architecture (#11, #17 residual); avoidance under imperfect compliance (#13); migration and the cross-base externality (#15); valuation route and assessment window adoption (#28); administrative-layer intervention effects (BEHAV-1); OBR independence empirical assessment (#22); and corporate instrument transition (#32). For each cluster it states the working assumption currently in force — the best available estimate in the absence of Phase One evidence — and specifies a prospective evaluation design: what data is required, where it comes from, what observation window is necessary, and what patterns in that data would constitute confirmation, revision, or contradiction of the working assumption.

The paper does not make design decisions. It specifies what Phase One measurement would produce evidence relevant to those decisions. Findings that pressure design choices flow back to the relevant companion paper as revisions.

Four limitations from the companion paper series are named as inherited: the pre-behavioural revenue figures in RATES (the most consequential, as the primary upper-bound starting point Phase One will correct); the high-growth boundary condition in VAL.A's simulation (understater penalties plateau at g ≈ 17% rather than reversing; the C.1 metric exceeding 100% at extreme growth is a normalisation artefact, not a sign reversal — a design boundary rather than a modelling error); the HMRC data access precondition for revenue microsimulation (#1, an institutional arrangement required before Phase One begins); and the jurisdiction-specific legal analysis of exit and bankruptcy closure (#8, BEHAV-4, CLOSE OQ 4) and corporate levy CIT interaction (#31), both assigned to the dedicated legal analysis paper and both assumed operational in the §5.3 and §5.7 measurement designs respectively.

The evaluation designs are written to be useful independently of whether Phase One happens on any particular timeline. They specify what would close each cluster; if the mechanism is never implemented, the paper stands as the honest account of what the series has and has not established.

---

## 14. The Environmental Effects and Transmission Channels Paper (ENV)

ENV is the paper that asks what the WDT does to the economy around it — distinct from the design papers, which ask how it works and why it takes the form it does. It does not produce a formal general equilibrium model and does not estimate magnitudes. Its contribution is to identify the correct transmission channels for this specific mechanism, distinguish them from the channels that standard wealth tax analysis assumes, and be explicit about where direction can be established analytically and where only Phase One can go further.

The paper's central reframing concerns the standard efficiency critique of wealth taxation — capital flight, investment chilling, lock-in at exit — which rests on the assumption that the tax is a friction on a capital stock. That assumption does not hold for a tax on the annual change in net worth with a symmetric loss refund. The correct starting point is that the existing tax architecture actively engineers capital stagnation and misdirection through lock-in distortions, basis step-up incentives, and debt preferences; the WDT removes those distortions rather than adding new ones. This aggregate friction removal is the primary efficiency argument and is logically prior to any Domar-Musgrave or use-it-or-lose-it claim.

The declaration equilibrium analysis in ENV §2 identifies a structural asymmetry in the mechanism's regret structure: understatement carries definite, compounding, unavoidable costs (deferred liability with no ceiling), while mild overstatement carries bounded, probabilistic costs. A rational risk-averse taxpayer consistently prefers mild overstatement. The population-level prediction is therefore systematic mild overstatement as the equilibrium declaration pattern rather than exact honest declaration — a finding that slightly offsets the behavioural response overstatement in RATES and that has an implication for SRR floor calibration (ENV-1).

The displacement channel (§4) was substantially expanded in ENV v0.3 and is now subsectioned (§4.1–§4.8). §4.1 (Staged Displacement) establishes that the LRR accumulation period is the mechanism through which the macroeconomic transition is managed: incremental annual disposable income increases of the order of £300–500 per worker do not generate inflationary shocks, reducing the transition risk that makes large fiscal reforms macroeconomically dangerous. §4.2 (The NICs Case) develops the bilateral National Insurance removal as the cleanest single transmission — both employer and employee sides removed simultaneously, the standard incidence ambiguity dissolved, the employment-relationship cost falling for both parties without bargaining complications. The two concerns in the policy literature (NICs removal accelerating gig-economy substitution and accelerating automation) both run the direction of effect backwards and are corrected.

§4.3–§4.8 (added v0.3) address automation and tax-base migration. The central observation is that artificial intelligence has the structural shape of a pervasive technological transition: substituting for cognitive as well as physical labour, operating across sectors rather than within one, and potentially outrunning the adaptive capacity of institutions calibrated to normal rates of economic change. A labour-based fiscal system faces a structural asymmetry under sustained automation: the production base can migrate from labour toward capital while the principal tax base remains attached to labour. The WDT reverses this relationship — as productive activity becomes increasingly capital-intensive, the WDT tax base becomes increasingly concentrated in the capital appreciation generated by that activity. §4.4 surveys five categories of existing policy response (reskilling, income floors, robot taxes, capital-income shift, ownership socialisation) and identifies the WDT's position within the relevant comparison class. §4.5 (Tax-Base Migration) states the structural claim: the WDT tracks productive capital appreciation regardless of how that appreciation was generated, providing fiscal resilience under different automation trajectories that labour-based systems cannot match mechanically. §4.6–§4.8 address household-level effects, extreme automation as a stress test, and what the WDT does not solve on this dimension. The quantitative relationship between automation trajectories, factor share dynamics, and relative revenue capacity is assigned to the MACRO modelling paper as ENV-4.

The consumption multiplier channel (§5) establishes that the RATES model is conservative along the growth-feedback dimension — the feedback loop from labour tax displacement to asset appreciation is real but uncredited in the RATES model — while simultaneously being overoptimistic on behavioural response. These biases move in opposite directions and their net effect is the open question assigned to the MACRO modelling paper (ENV-3).

The financial stability analysis (§6) establishes that the symmetric refund mechanism has stabilising properties in financial downturns that the mechanism was not designed to produce: it reaches the population whose portfolio decisions move asset markets and dampens the forced-selling mechanism that amplifies liquidity spirals. The SWF holds a potential countercyclical deployment capacity not currently in GOV.B's mandate architecture, identified as a named potential extension rather than settled design.

The inflation response and countercyclical architecture section (§7) identifies two independent automatic countercyclical instruments — Route C equity rotation into low-correlation assets, and labour relief disbursement pace adjustment — operating through independent channels so that a Governing Council that cannot agree on one lever can still activate the other. The DR chamber's pre-commitment capacity changes the political economy of countercyclical restraint in a specific way: pre-committed future acceleration under documented trigger conditions converts what is otherwise a unilateral government promise into something closer to a contract with a counterparty holding genuine enforcement capacity. A parameter clarification to GOV.B's Custodian mandate is implied: adding explicit guidance on accelerated Route C rotation pace under defined inflationary trigger conditions converts automatic countercyclical effect into deliberate policy.

The housing analysis (§8) identifies a distributional improvement from demand composition shift — speculative demand falling, owner-occupier demand rising — that standard price-level analysis does not capture. The WDT's contribution to the housing problem is demand composition, not supply; the binding planning constraint is unaffected.

ENV Appendix A reframes OQ #9 from a pre-Phase One general equilibrium modelling task into a Phase One successor: a macroeconomic modelling paper (MACRO) to be written using ENV's channel characterisations as structural framework and Phase One evidence as empirical inputs. The four sub-questions in OQ #9 are addressed directionally in ENV; their magnitude quantification requires the MACRO paper.

ENV generates four open questions: ENV-1 (consumption multiplier magnitude and SRR calibration implication — Phase One), ENV-2 (housing price net effect — Phase One), ENV-3 (net bias direction of RATES estimates — MACRO paper), and ENV-4 (automation and tax-base migration — MACRO paper, companion question to ENV-3).

## 15. The First Mover Paper (FM)

FM is a strategic analysis paper. It does not design or modify any WDT mechanism. Its subject is the adoption dynamics that follow from the WDT's properties if those properties hold as the companion series claims.

The paper's central argument is a conditional binary: if the WDT works as described, any jurisdiction that has concluded this is likely true faces a choice with no stable intermediate option. Either commit to full implementation before first-mover advantages begin accruing elsewhere, or ensure they never begin accruing anywhere. The conditionality is load-bearing — the paper explicitly identifies four premises that generate the binary, each evaluable independently, and states that the conclusion does not apply if any one fails. The premises are: first-mover gains compound in ways late movers cannot recover; partial implementation is not available (non-decomposability); the mechanism works as described; and the implementation minimum is real (Phase One cannot be compressed by political urgency).

Non-decomposability is what closes the apparent middle option of partial adoption. The paper argues this at length for each of the three most likely targets for omission. Removing the symmetric refund destroys both the valuation architecture's self-balancing property (the penalty for understatement in loss years disappears) and the Domar-Musgrave risk-sharing claim. Removing the constitutional governance structure reproduces the hollowing dynamic that ended prior OECD wealth taxes — incremental revision until the mechanism is no longer the same instrument. Removing the sovereign wealth fund converts the refund from a mechanically pre-funded obligation into a promise backed only by future revenue. In each case the result is a different system with known failure modes, not a weaker version of the WDT. A partial imitation that fails is attributed to the WDT in the public record even though the mechanism implemented was not the WDT; FM identifies this as the most damaging outcome available to those who prefer the current system, more damaging than open opposition.

On what first-mover commitment delivers: the SRR reaches its target capitalisation floor within three years under every historical starting condition in the UK equity return dataset (RATES), at which point the refund guarantee becomes mechanically credible rather than aspirational. Efficiency gains from removing lock-in distortions, basis step-up incentives, and debt preferences begin accruing through the transition period. At the median of fourteen years the LRR reaches its floor and labour tax displacement begins at scale. Internationally mobile wealth moves toward the first-mover jurisdiction because it has become the most rational place to hold significant wealth — loss protection available nowhere else, lower friction than alternatives, a privacy election that removes the non-tax reasons for complex offshore structuring. The first mover also acquires time: valuation infrastructure, adviser ecosystem knowledge, and behavioural evidence that later movers cannot replicate without going through the same process from scratch. Revenue figures across the companion series are pre-behavioural; FM states this plainly and frames the first-mover commitment as a bet that the mechanism's design properties reduce departure enough that gains exceed losses, with RATES's coverage ratios suggesting substantial margin.

On the suppression strategy: the paper characterises it as coherent and rational, not requiring coordination or bad faith. Actors whose position depends on the current system have aligned rational interests in preventing demonstration. The suppression strategy operates primarily through the scrutiny period — before Phase One has proven the mechanism's properties, when every claim in the companion series is still theoretical. Policy advisers raise apparent commitment risk; think tanks produce partial alternatives that appear to address the same problems; treasury officials resist the constitutional governance structure as a constraint on ministerial discretion. Partial imitation is identified as the most dangerous form of suppression: harder to identify than opposition, attributable to the WDT's own failure if it fails, and operating through the normal channels of policy development without requiring any actor to be explicitly working against the proposal.

The paper closes with a dated record of its own predictions: the binary equilibrium had not resolved at the time of writing; no jurisdiction had implemented the WDT; the dynamics described were analytical predictions, not observations. The intellectual record is preserved so that two things remain possible regardless of what happens — verification of the predictions against events as they unfold, and reconstruction by a future designer if the proposal is successfully suppressed before demonstration.

FM generates no open questions and closes none in the consolidated register.

## 16. The Modular Adoption Paper (MOD)

MOD is a strategic analysis paper. It does not design or modify any WDT mechanism. Its subject is the adoption pathway that results from the fact that some WDT enabling infrastructure also attracts independent justification outside the WDT.

The paper begins with a distinction between two categories of WDT institution. Category 1 consists of enabling infrastructure that the WDT requires and that also carries independent justification entirely outside the WDT: a national valuation profession with published standards, a public valuation register, beneficial ownership attribution law, a sovereign wealth fund in the generic sense, and independent fiscal governance in the generic sense. Category 2 consists of mechanisms that are constitutively WDT-specific and have no independent justification outside the full architecture: the symmetric refund at the marginal tax rate, the declaration equilibrium, the Route D auction, the lifetime contribution envelope, and the three-chamber Governing Council structure.

The modular adoption thesis is bounded: it applies to Category 1 only. Non-decomposability (established in FM §2) confirms that the WDT cannot stand without its Category 1 institutions; MOD's claim runs in the opposite direction — some Category 1 institutions can stand without the WDT, and the relationship is asymmetric. A jurisdiction that assembles Category 1 infrastructure through locally rational policy decisions has not adopted the WDT and cannot arrive at it by institutional drift alone. The remaining Category 2 commitment still requires a deliberate political decision. What has changed is the size of that remaining step.

Three independent policy currents produce Category 1 infrastructure without any WDT champion being required. The global push for beneficial ownership transparency builds attribution law and public asset registers for financial crime and anti-corruption reasons. The pursuit of fiscal credibility and intergenerational saving produces sovereign wealth funds and independent fiscal institutions that are formally distinct from but structurally adjacent to the WDT's SWF and Governing Council. Professional reform in the valuation market — driven by property taxation, inheritance tax, and transfer pricing needs — produces the professional valuation infrastructure the WDT's four-route architecture requires. Infrastructure creates interests, and those interests advocate forward. The mechanism that connects all three currents is the same: each produces constituencies that want their infrastructure extended into new applications, regardless of whether those constituencies know the WDT exists.

MOD distinguishes its thesis from FM's binary. FM addresses a government that has evaluated the WDT and is choosing between commit and suppress. MOD addresses governments and policy communities that have not yet evaluated the WDT and are making infrastructure decisions for independent reasons. The modular adoption pathway is not an alternative to the binary; it describes the terrain on which that binary will eventually be confronted. A jurisdiction with mature Category 1 infrastructure faces a smaller remaining commitment when it does evaluate the WDT. Separately, MOD notes that infrastructure accretion is harder to suppress than a single identifiable proposal, since the communities defending each Category 1 institution have reasons to do so unrelated to the WDT. This does not make suppression impossible; it means some of the infrastructure suppression would need to prevent is being built for reasons entirely outside the WDT's intellectual project.

MOD generates no open questions and closes none in the consolidated register.
